newsitem.title: USA: Clinton backs U.S. news organizations for Cuba.
newsitem.headline: Clinton backs U.S. news organizations for Cuba.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday granted permission to some of America's largest news organisations to open bureaus in Cuba with the aim of bringing pressure for democratic change in Havana.
But it was unclear whether communist-ruled Cuba would approve any moves other than to let Cable News Network (CNN) open a bureau.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the decision was in keeping with President Bill Clinton's stated policy to support an "increased flow of accurate information to and from and within Cuba itself."

"The administration believes that news gathering and reporting by U.S. news organisations will keep international attention focused on the situation in Cuba and the realities of economic and political conditions there and will bring greater public exposure to those who are advocating a democratic change in Cuba," McCurry told reporters.

Licenses valid for one year were granted to television networks CNN, CBS and ABC, the Associated Press wire service, newspapers the Miami Herald, the Sun-Sentinel of Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and the Chicago Tribune, the news agency and newspaper group Dow Jones, and the Spanish-language television network Univision.
A license also went to CubaINFO, a newsletter associated with the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies.
McCurry said approval was granted to all news organisations having applications with the Treasury Department.

All but CNN must seek approval from the Cuban government to set up operations in Havana. Cuban President Fidel Castro's government announced in November it was granting permission to CNN to set up a bureau.

A Cuban Foreign Ministry official in Havana gave no indication when or whether other U.S. news organisations would be granted approval to open offices. U.S. journalists who visit the island now must obtain a special visa.
Analysts doubted that Castro would move quickly to welcome a tidal wave of American journalists because the Cuban leader has expressed displeasure in the past about negative U.S. television reports.

"I don't think there's going to be a rush," said Larry Birns of the Council on Hemispheric Affairs. "This has no particular advantages for Castro. The very fact that the administration is doing this suggests that it is not a good deal for the Cuban government."

In Miami, the most powerful Cuban exile group, the Cuban American National Foundation, welcomed the U.S. move. Spokeswoman Ninoska Perez said exiles would be pleased to have independent reports from their homeland.
"We would like to see it covered from an angle other than the government's," she said. "So many things are happening in Cuba and sometimes correspondents there now look the other way."
But two Cuban-born Republican members of Congress from Florida, Reps. Ileana Ros-Lehtinen and Lincoln Diaz-Balart, were sceptical.

"I am concerned that U.S. media organisations will not be able to have free access to all areas of Cuba and instead be carefully guided by Castro's propaganda operatives to show only the news coverage that Castro wants to broadcast," Ros-Lehtinen said.

U.S. policy toward Cuba has been under fire around the world. Under pressure from U.S. allies, Clinton had to suspend a key clause of the Helms-Burton law that would penalise foreign companies doing business with properties confiscated from Americans in Cuba.

Clinton had announced in October 1995 that he would allow U.S. news organisations to open offices in Havana for the first time in more than three decades. But a formal decision was delayed by the February 1996 shooting down of two Florida-based civilian aircraft by the Cuban air force.
